Nvidia's board of directors has established a national security and export control oversight committee in response to growing scrutiny from the United States over how the company handled exports of its chips to companies linked to China. Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones stated that "advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," adding that NVIDIA "recognises" these challenges while affirming the company's responsibility and opportunity to lead in addressing them, with a commitment to working constructively with government and industry partners to establish a robust framework safeguarding national security. The new committee will oversee Nvidia's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management; it is set to meet quarterly, including with management and in executive session, while retaining independent outside experts in law, national security, and trade compliance.

The committee comes amid the recent resignation of Nvidia cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Prior to his departure, Huang had cultivated a close relationship with Trump, serving as a key voice for the US on artificial intelligence while also lobbying for permission to allow chip exports to China. In connection with these matters, Nvidia launched an investigation into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy; however, the board stated last week that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Separately, on Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled an interim final rule targeting remote access to advanced computing chips and servers through overseas data centres. The article contains no specific quantities or figures beyond these reported events and statements.
items.title: Nvidia Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee Amid Jensen Huang Resignation

items.summary:
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee in the wake of the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to employees; one affair involved a woman suspected of spying for China while helping ensure higher-quality AI chips reached the Chinese market, according to reports seemingly based on US intelligence that these suspicions had been known for roughly a year.

The events have heightened oversight concerns about Nvidia and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month. The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, which will meet at least once every quarter and incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts. Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair it, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, and John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). Nvidia already has lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team groups that will report to this board-level committee.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous. US President Donald Trump welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines Tuesday during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell.

The scandal has also highlighted questions about US-China chip trade. Huang was influential in persuading Trump to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other companies deemed prudent. One affair involved a woman who used to lead Megaspseed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing company and major Nvidia client suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls; intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
items.title: Nvidia Forms National Security Committee After Jensen Huang Scandal

items.summary:
The US technology firm Apple is to stand trial in Paris beginning June 17 on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets. French prosecutors brought charges against Apple Distribution International and its parent company, Apple Inc, alleging that they obstructed repair and refurbishment for more than two and a half years, from November 2021 to July 2024. The alleged practice involved configuring software so it was impossible to repair or refurbish the phones outside Apple's authorised network; for example, Face ID might be disabled if an unauthorised shop replaced the camera, or the battery health feature could stop working. Affected models range from the iPhone XS and the iPhone 12, 13, 14 and 15 series to the iPhone SE released in 2022.

If found guilty, Apple could face fines of up to €300,000 plus an additional fine of up to 5% of its annual revenue — which would roughly be €21.7 billion as of publication — and compensation claims from clients. The company contests the allegations as unfounded. This case follows earlier settlements: in February 2021 Apple agreed to pay €25 million for failing to tell iPhone users that software updates could slow down older devices, a settlement among several worldwide after Apple admitted in December 2017 that its iOS operating software was slowing the performance of older phones whose battery life was deteriorating. The alleged aim behind this case was reportedly to boost sales and increase revenue; Apple now generates more than $400 billion a year, with roughly half coming from iPhone sales.
items.title: Apple Faces Landmark Planned-Obsolescence Trial in France

items.summary:
The Up First newsletter opens with United Airlines disruptions stemming from the Federal Aviation Administration's Friday nationwide ground stop, which occurred as air travel returned to normal after that halt. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA will reevaluate future maintenance procedures, while former FAA senior executive Mike McCormick told NPR's Joe Hernandez he believes another nationwide ground stop is unlikely; McCormick noted the FAA sometimes imposes a temporary maintenance moratorium in such cases. The incident happened as L3Harris workers converted copper wires to fiber optic and installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.

The briefing then shifts to President Trump, who is in Manila today for an ASEAN summit with allies before traveling tomorrow to Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever joint summit of Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. That meeting will occur on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen. Although Ukraine was previously announced as not being on the agenda for the trilateral meeting, Trump said yesterday he would discuss his "favorite subject": Ukraine when leaving the White House. Europe and Ukraine are concerned about how Ukraine may be discussed given President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not attend APEC and Trump has recently grown more lenient toward Putin and Russia.

The final major story concerns Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose resignation has shaken Silicon Valley and prompted calls from tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. An online petition supporting his reinstatement has garnered more than 160,000 signatures, though NPR's Shannon Bond says some may not be real; Elon Musk says he signed it. Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital, a key Nvidia investor, urged the board to thoroughly investigate and keep all options open. Many prominent AI and venture capital figures recognize Huang as a visionary whose company played a significant role in the AI boom.

A shorter deep dive examines New Mexico's universal free childcare program, which became the first state to offer such benefits to all families regardless of income one year ago, provided adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Only 50% of some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled, with a nearly $600 million operating budget that some lawmakers fear could run about $50 million over this year. New Mexico state Sen. Steve Lanier supports universal childcare only for some people, citing steep costs; since the program's enactment, lower-income mothers' full-time employment has risen by 23%, according to a new Arizona State University paper.

The picture show notes that millions of shorebirds migrate annually to Alaska to breed, though nearly half of the 41 Alaskan-breeding species are in decline as climate change disrupts their timing with peak insect availability. Finally, three things to know: British actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh James Bond; RAYE leads Grammy Award nominations with 11 nods, followed by Rosalía with nine; and civil rights champion Dolores Huerta became the first non-elected individual and first woman to lie in honor at the California State Capitol before dying of cancer last month at age 96.
items.title: Trump's Asia Summit and Nvidia's Huang Reinstatement Drive a Tech-Heavy Up First Briefing

items.summary: At a dedicated session at COP31 in Turkiye, International Energy Agency deputy executive director Mary Bruce Warlick warned that global renewable energy growth is likely to fall short of the goal of tripling output by 2030 without immediate policy intervention. She said renewables are expected to grow by around 4,800 gigawatts from 2026 to 2031 and reach approximately 9,710 gigawatts by 2030 — about 2.6 times the 2022 level but below the tripling target — even as their share of global electricity generation rises from one-third to nearly 45%. Warlick urged governments to close the gap and hit the goal by late 2031 through immediate procurement tenders, reforming permission processes, and investing in grid modernization and battery storage. She emphasized that energy efficiency must improve by 4% per year through 2030 (up from 1% and 2% improvement rates in 2024 and 2025), which would require an additional $1.3 trillion in annual worldwide investment, though she noted such capital could lower bills and boost national energy security over time. Warlick stressed that the goals will not be reached unless clean energy investments accelerate globally, especially in emerging and developing countries. Separately, Amanda Ohara, senior energy advisor for the COP30 Presidency of Brazil, warned that infrastructure shortages are the primary obstacle to phasing out fossil fuels, calling on countries to develop investment roadmaps balancing climate mandates with economic priorities.
items.title: IEA Deputy Chief Warns Global Renewable Growth May Miss 2030 Tripling Target

items.summary: CGTN's Tian Wei attended the APEC CEO Summit held in Shenzhen and interviewed Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who described the event as a great experience. The president expressed hope for sharing insights and achievements with countries across the region during his participation in the summit.
items.title: Chilean President at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen

items.summary: The Business Council of Canada projects that approximately 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles will enter the Canadian market by the end of this year. According to an editor's note, Goldy Hyder, President and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, stated that Canada will permit these vehicles into its market within the current year. Hyder sees strong potential for expanded cooperation between the two nations, particularly in investment. He emphasized that Canadian businesses are no newcomers to the Chinese market, noting as he said "We've been here a long time" and stressing that they have established presence there.
items.title: Business Council of Canada: 49,000 Chinese EVs expected in Canada

items.summary:
Climate change, extreme weather and the energy transition are pressing challenges across the Asia-Pacific that no single economy can address alone. Aligned with the APEC Putrajaya Vision 2040, regional players are leveraging their respective resource endowments to build practical partnerships advancing low-carbon growth.

Green industrial capacity and technology cooperation is taking shape through concrete projects. In Indonesia, the Cirata floating solar plant—described as one of Southeast Asia's largest facilities of its kind—has come online to supply clean power to the grid; built by Chinese contractors, it demonstrates how photovoltaic technology can be adapted for reservoir sites in tropical APEC economies. Chinese battery firms have also established supporting manufacturing lines within Indonesia's industrial zones, forming integrated upstream and downstream clusters for the electric vehicle supply chain.

In Thailand, BYD's Rayong plant carries an annual capacity of 150,000 units and serves as a regional manufacturing hub for right-hand-drive new-energy vehicles. The facility has attracted a cluster of component suppliers for batteries, motors and charging equipment, nurturing local manufacturing jobs and technical know-how.

For Pacific island economies on the front line of climate risks, shared satellite observation data has become a critical early-warning tool. China's Fengyun meteorological satellites provide continuous high-frequency remote sensing data to support climate monitoring, tropical cyclone tracking and disaster forecasting for these nations. Under the China-Pacific Island Countries climate cooperation initiative rolled out in 2025, Fengyun data services are open to Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea and Tonga. The satellite system tracked volcanic ash plumes during the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption and supported emergency hazard assessments for subsequent disaster responses. This service is part of wider efforts under the UN Early Warnings for All initiative to close the early-warning gap in small island developing states.

Digital tools are also helping APEC economies make regional value chains more transparent and low-carbon. APEC trade and investment working groups have piloted digital traceability systems jointly by China, Indonesia and Peru to verify environmental and social credentials of traded goods; the pilot schemes cover coffee, timber and textile products. Using shared digital standards, producers, exporters and regulators can trace commodity origins, record carbon footprints and check compliance with sustainability criteria. The framework reduces repetitive compliance checks and helps certified green goods access markets across APEC more smoothly.

Under inclusive technology transfer and peer learning during the APEC Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, delegates and industry participants stress that sustainable transition pathways differ widely—shaped by each economy's natural resources, energy mix and development stage. The Putrajaya Vision 2040 sets the long-term direction for an open, resilient Asia-Pacific community. Progress on sustainability relies on voluntary multilateral coordination, accessible technology transfer and peer learning rather than uniform regulatory requirements; economies are encouraged to share mature low-carbon solutions and tailor them to local conditions instead of adopting identical green transition roadmaps.

As the APEC "China Year" enters its Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, these on-the-ground projects illustrate a core message: shared climate risks call for shared solutions. Inclusive technology access, capacity building and collaborative trade frameworks will translate the APEC sustainability commitments into tangible benefits for communities across the region.
items.title: Asia-Pacific cooperation for a greener future: APEC's low-carbon partnerships under Putrajaya Vision 2040

items.summary:
On Monday, November 16, 2026, thousands of customers across the United States reported difficulties accessing banking services and completing transactions. The disruption stemmed from a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that caused delays involving multiple financial institutions. An ATM machine displayed a 'not working' screen at a Chase bank in Irving, Texas, illustrating the impact on physical branch operations.

Customers encountered problems with online and mobile banking services at several major banks, including Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank. Some also experienced delays when sending or receiving payments through Zelle, a popular peer-to-peer payment service. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a temporary software bug in its on-premise hardware systems had slowed the processing of some transactions.

The bank reassured customers that they could still access their accounts and funds, and there was no evidence that the issue was related to a cyberattack. The disruption produced knock-on effects on other financial institutions when they were involved in transactions with Chase. However, JPMorgan stressed that the incident was not systemic. US Bank noted its own systems were not directly affected, while some customers might still experience delays with cross-bank Zelle payments.

Early Warning Services, Zelle's operator, confirmed that its payment network remained fully operational throughout the disruption. The situation improved later on Monday; at around 6:30 p.m. Eastern Time, a Chase spokesperson said transactions were posting normally again, indicating that the main disruption had been resolved.
items.title: JPMorgan Software Bug Triggers Banking Delays Across US

items.summary: The UK has sanctioned eight construction and property development firms in what it describes as the first package of measures since its government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank. The sanctions target companies involved in building settlements, which the UK says are illegal under international law, with the aim of disrupting their flows of finance and ability to support settlement construction. This move comes amid a reported sharp rise in settlement construction over recent years and a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property since the start of the Gaza war, triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza. The measures follow a broader expansion last month of the UK's human rights sanctions regime, enabling it to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world. Separately, the government is developing legislation to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements and advertising services for settlement properties in the UK. This announcement comes two days before the deadline for bids on construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem, plans which would effectively divide the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband warned that such development would render a two-state solution unviable by cutting through the heart of Palestine, describing the status quo as unacceptable while expressing commitment to working with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority toward lasting peace. Israel has yet to comment but has previously condemned UK sanctions over West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of systematically acting against the State of Israel; in September 2024 it announced its own ban on importing settlement goods and acting against companies supporting settlement expansion, prompting a furious Israeli reaction that included closing the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Since occupying the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews, alongside whom an estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live.
items.title: UK Sanctions Firms Over Israeli West Bank Settlements

items.summary: The UK government has appointed Alan Milburn as chair of a new Youth Opportunities Unit, which will sit at the centre of government reporting directly to the prime minister. The unit is tasked with shaping the cross-government response to the Milburn review, reducing NEET rates, delivering the Youth Opportunity and Support Guarantee, mobilising partners beyond central government, and drawing on data and insight to improve delivery.
items.title: Milburn's Youth Opportunities Unit and reactions to welfare cuts

items.summary: CGTN's program Green Electrostate explores how artificial intelligence is reshaping global power demand as it transforms the world at an accelerating pace. Behind every AI breakthrough lies electricity, and AI continues to grow increasingly hungry for more of it, pushing power grids worldwide toward their limits. In China specifically, two forces are gaining momentum: the rise of AI alongside the growth of renewable energy—developments whose futures appear destined to collide as they reshape the geography of computing. The episode travels to Ulanqab, a city located on windswept grasslands far from China's largest technology hubs, yet it has emerged into international headlines as an emerging hotspot for artificial intelligence. Through this journey, Green Electrostate examines how power systems built in yesterday's world can adapt to meet the demands of tomorrow.
items.title: Green Electrostate: Powering the AI Age

items.summary:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay, publishing its decision on Tuesday. The court ordered Turkey to release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament, finding that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism. It also ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation. The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately but rather within the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights, yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in cases involving rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas. As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey as well as freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers. He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup." Continuing his struggle from Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections. A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court. His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament. Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail. After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.
items.title: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay

items.summary: According to CNN's reporting on Tuesday, November 17, a highly classified network used by the U.S. National Security Agency for its internal communications has gone down. The agency was working at the time to understand the scope of the problem, and there was no immediate evidence pointing to a cyberattack as the cause. CNN cited five people familiar with the matter in connection with the report. When seeking comment about the reported outage, the NSA did not immediately respond.
items.title: Highly Classified US National Security Communications Network Is Down

items.summary:
At this year's U.N. climate summit (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye—running from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20, 2026—the conference is billed as an 'implementation' gathering focused on turning prior agreements into action rather than issuing sweeping new pledges. Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on about 161 million hectares (400 million acres) in tropical forest countries, effectively provide $1.8 billion in funding, and respect free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. These demands come amid a recent U.N. report warning that limiting global warming to 1.5°C (2.4°F)—the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement—will be virtually impossible.

The summit follows last year's gathering in Belém, Brazil, which drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance and was dubbed 'the Indigenous COP,' though it was also marked by frustration over a long-standing pattern of exclusion. Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, noted that it remains a struggle to determine whether further progress will be made in realizing Indigenous rights.

Climate-driven threats have intensified recently: massive floods and landslides in Nepal killed more than 1,500 people; an intense wildfire season in Canada burned millions of hectares; and wildfire smoke in Indonesia caused thousands of deaths across Southeast Asia. A historically powerful El Niño further threatens famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes globally.

Funding remains a key priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage provisionally disbursed $21.6 million for Nepal—its first disbursement and less than 1% of the approximately $4 billion to $5 billion in damage the country sustained. Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster.

Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, attends COP31 partly to highlight the landmark climate case her father, Mike Smith, led against major emitters using Māori customary law—a case blocked by the national government. Quack Pirihi, a Māori activist speaking on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change, emphasized that for over 30 years Indigenous knowledges have been brought to negotiations, yet emissions continue to rise.

As negotiations continue through Nov. 20, advocates insist discussions must lead to tangible actions rather than mere commitments.
items.title: Indigenous Leaders Press for Action at COP31 Climate Summit

items.summary:
Rhett Ayers Butler, founder and CEO of Mongabay, argues in this commentary that independent journalism plays an often-overlooked role in conservation by providing credible information, exposing problems, amplifying local voices, and helping successful approaches gain recognition. He contends that conservation philanthropy should invest more in such reporting even though its impact is difficult to measure.

Butler illustrates the value of investigative reporting with a 2021 tip from a source in Sabah, Malaysia, about a proposed carbon credit deal covering some 2 million hectares (5 million acres) of rainforest. The relationship with that source had been built over 15 years; it trusted Mongabay to protect its identity and verify the information. Butlers notes the more troubling issue was that senior Sabah officials were negotiating with a Singapore company incorporated just two years earlier, with only $1,000 in paid-up capital and no demonstrated track record of managing conservation on such a scale. Indigenous communities whose customary rights could be affected had not been meaningfully consulted, potentially locking their ancestral land into an opaque contract for more than a century.

The timing proved consequential: a Malaysian delegation was planning to market the project's carbon credits at the U.N. climate conference in Glasgow, Scotland. When the story broke and made headlines in Malaysia and beyond, those plans fell apart. In February 2022, the agreement was declared legally unenforceable in its existing form, and by 2024 it had been effectively blocked.

Butler observes that conservation organizations spend billions of dollars every year on fieldwork and advancing policy, yet far less goes to independent reporting even though it is often how local voices get elevated. He notes that philanthropic foundations judge grantees on quantitative metrics like hectares conserved, people trained, animals vaccinated, and trees planted, while scientists can measure changes in tree cover, soundscape complexity, tiger detections, or water quality recovery. These measures reveal little about who made decisions, how they were reached, who was engaged, or what happens when the interests of conservation organizations, governments, and communities diverge.

Drawing on more than quarter of a century at Mongabay, Butler explains that much reporting occurs in places where governance is weak, public information is scarce, land and resource decisions face limited scrutiny, and impunity is common. He cites 2024 findings that companies had persuaded Indigenous communities in Peru, Bolivia, and Panama to sign agreements surrendering economic rights connected to more than 9.5 million hectares (23.5 million acres) of ancestral forests. Mongabay's reporting led by Gloria Pallares undermined the projects' claims; after learning of these findings, the Matsés community in Peru terminated its agreement and Conservation International ended a memorandum of understanding with one company.

Butler emphasizes that ecological gains alone are insufficient when conservation depends on community cooperation, since resentment from exclusion can undermine protected areas. Local journalists are often best equipped to spot tensions because they understand local politics, customary rights, past disputes, and traditional practices. Reporting relies on relationships built over years with people who would never speak to an outsider.

For philanthropists, Butler argues that independent journalism has value well beyond raising awareness: it can identify risks before they become serious and reveal shortcomings in widely accepted approaches. Funders cannot dictate which stories get pursued or their conclusions; once a funder steers coverage away from its own investments, the reporting stops being useful. The independence that allows journalists to expose problems also makes their accounts of conservation successes more credible.

He offers a recent example from Gabon: the community of Massaha campaigned to protect its ancestral forest, known as Ibola Dja Bana Ba Massaha, from a logging concession operated by a foreign company. After a scientist reached out, Mongabay asked a Gabonese journalist to investigate; Benjamin Evine-Binet's story brought the dispute to an international audience and prompted the country's environment minister to visit the site. He found irregularities in the logging company's permit and revoked it, with the community now working toward official recognition of its forest as a community-conserved area.

Butler acknowledges that journalism's impact is usually harder to pin down: stories may inform regulatory decisions months later or provide evidence for court cases, prompt investigations into malpractice, or introduce associations to new approaches. Sometimes nothing follows publication, and there are important stories whose effects can never be measured. Funders accustomed to numerical targets and fixed deadlines often find this hard to evaluate; Mongabay tracks readership and republication but also follows up with reporters and sources years later.

He concludes that much of the reporting takes place in regions where few independent journalists cover environmental issues, some investigations require months of work and reach relatively small audiences, yet they still commit resources without guaranteeing outcomes. He hopes funders will do the same.
items.title: Why conservation needs independent journalism (commentary)

items.summary:
This weekend Estonia announced that as of December 1 all of its border crossings with Russia would close, a decision Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said was driven by “clear evidence” that the Russian military intelligence agency GRU had been behind a failed sabotage attack on a drone factory in northern Estonia. In his post on X, Tsahkna argued the closure would reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities and strengthen efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention. Prime Minister Kristen Michal framed the move as a firm response — “the opposite” of what he said was Russia’s aim to make Estonians afraid and weaken their support for Ukraine — sending a message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry are unacceptable.

Experts, however, questioned whether closing the border actually matters in an era when hybrid warfare increasingly relies on cyber tools rather than physical incursions. Anton Shekhovtsov, director of the Centre for Democratic Integrity in Austria and a Russia specialist, noted there were no direct links between the botched sabotage operation and the border closure, pointing out that none of the eight suspects arrested was Russian — they are all Latvian nationals who crossed into Estonia via other borders. He described how hybrid operations have been “uberised,” with operatives recruited online for individual assignments; he cited the 2024 attempted assassination of Bulgarian journalist Christo Grozev in the UK, and this summer’s incursion of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig Airport, where suspects reportedly reached Germany via Serbia and Turkey. Grossfield called it a trend toward on-demand operators working remotely.

On the risks side, Shekhovtsov warned that Russian agents have strong ties to organised crime networks in Europe — he pointed to the September attack on a Starlink ground station in Poland carried out by a Turkish criminal network commissioned by Russian intelligence. Grossfield cautioned that Estonians with family or businesses across the border could be affected and become easier for spies to approach, though she acknowledged it might “complicate communication and the transport of materials” and make sabotage more expensive. Shekhovtsov suggested domestic politics played a role: while Finland closed its border three years ago, he said Estonia may have been looking for an excuse to do the same ahead of parliamentary elections in March.

The article concludes that even if the closure makes Russian operations “more complicated,” it is unlikely to stop them altogether. Grossfield noted the shuttering sends a powerful political signal but does not prevent authorities from taking more targeted measures behind the scenes, and Shekhovtsov agreed it remains probably the best way to counter Russia — though he conceded closing the border won’t prevent Russian intelligence agencies from continuing to target Estonia as they have done up until now. The piece was adapted from an original French-language article.
items.title: Estonia closes its border with Russia amid hybrid-warfare fears — but can it keep Moscow out?

items.summary: The US government confirmed an investigation into Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed over suspected violations of export controls involving advanced semiconductors, with renewed scrutiny focused on the firm's alleged role in helping Chinese companies access Nvidia AI chips. The Departments of Commerce and Justice announced the matter on Monday (November 16), noting that the Commerce Department had launched its investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after identifying suspicious activity linked to potential diversion of sensitive semiconductor technology. Investigators sought records from Nvidia in May 2025 concerning direct or indirect sales of chips to Megaspeed, and subsequently placed the Singapore-based company on a 'no sell' list in June 2025. In that same month, US officials working with Singaporean law enforcement conducted an on-site end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed its then CEO, Alice Huang. The investigation has not established any wrongdoing or disclosed charges against the firm, though the Justice Department is leading the criminal probe alongside Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security.
items.title: US Investigation of Singapore's Megaspeed Over Suspected Nvidia Chip Diversion to China

items.summary: Nvidia shares fell roughly 24% this month after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, prompting Colette Kress to take over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. The selloff coincided with Nvidia's third-quarter earnings—the first without Huang at the helm—and amid broader AI-sector volatility driven by skepticism about hyperscaler capex plans. Despite the turmoil, UBS maintained its Buy rating on Nvidia and cut its target price from $300 to $240 per share, which still implies around 54% upside from the stock's previous closing price of $156.14. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri argued that market assumptions are overly draconian—projecting a peak in 2028 with EBITDA margins compressing by 1,500 basis points—and unlikely to hold given Nvidia's momentum for at least two more years even without Huang as CEO.
items.title: UBS Sees 54% Nvidia Upside Despite Huang Scandal and Share Crash

items.summary:
On November 17 in New Delhi, chipmaker NVIDIA announced the creation of a new standing Board of Directors committee called the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The release stated that this body is responsible for board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. Existing NVIDIA teams—the National Security team and the Global Trade Compliance team—are set to report directly to the new committee as well as to Interim CEO Colette Kress. Committee leadership includes director Suzanne Nora Johnson as chair, with Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri serving as members. The committee is scheduled to meet at least once every quarter, including sessions with management and executive sessions.

The company framed the decision as reflecting the Board's further commitment to enhancing engagement with relevant government stakeholders and demonstrating high standards of governance. NVIDIA noted that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented national security challenges, positioning itself as the world's leading advanced computing company responsible for addressing them while supporting continued technological innovation.

In a separate development, NVIDIA, IBM, and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) collaborated to develop a modular quantum computing codesign platform that combines quantum processors with accelerated computing systems. Under the initiative, NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will be installed alongside IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM described as its most powerful quantum processor to date. The jointly developed platform is intended to enable researchers to develop and test error-correction codes, decoding algorithms, and applications integrating quantum and classical computing.

The article was auto-generated from an agency feed and has not been edited by FPJ's editorial team.
items.title: NVIDIA Establishes National Security Oversight Committee and Partners With IBM on Quantum Computing Research

items.summary: On Tuesday, Amazon announced plans to invest $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, significantly expanding its carbon-free energy portfolio and supporting the country's transition toward a more sustainable and resilient energy future. This new commitment adds to the $4 billion already contracted in Indian renewable investments, making Amazon one of India's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy. The announcement includes four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 megawatts (MW). These include a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka—Amazon's largest wind project contracted in Asia to date; a 200 MW combined solar-and-wind project in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. Secured through Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), these projects are part of Amazon's existing $4 billion contracted portfolio, and once operational will have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts—enough to generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households. The investment supports Amazon's new global goal to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030, meaning every unit of electricity consumed will be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions than in 2019. This target represents a milestone on the path to Amazon's Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040. Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi welcomed the investment, noting it advances India's clean energy ambitions, strengthens energy security, supports sustainable economic growth, and reflects global companies' growing confidence in India's renewable sector. Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon, emphasized that this additional $7 billion underscores their long-term commitment to bringing more wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India's energy security and renewable ambitions.
items.title: Amazon's $7 Billion Renewable Energy Investment in India by 2030

items.summary:
Nvidia is set to report its fiscal third-quarter results after the US stock market closes, arriving at a difficult moment for what analysts describe as the world's most valuable chipmaker. The company has benefited from enormous spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure by major technology companies whose graphics processing units power data centres used to train and operate AI models. Analysts expect quarterly revenue of approximately $109 billion, representing another substantial increase from the previous year. Data centre revenue deserves particular attention as this segment has become the main driver of Nvidia's business while Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta continue investing in AI computing capacity.

Leadership uncertainty looms large over the company following Jensen Huang's departure, which created questions about leadership and future direction after he played a central role in transforming Nvidia from a graphics processor manufacturer into a major force in the global AI industry. CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while the board looks for a permanent replacement; reports indicate the board is not considering bringing Huang back.

The market context reflects broader turbulence, with Nvidia stock falling 24% and shares losing almost a quarter of their value in November before dropping another 4.1% on Monday, November 16 as investors reduced exposure ahead of earnings. The decline affected other semiconductor companies including AMD, Micron Technology and Sandisk as investors reconsidered valuations across the AI sector amid concerns about high prices for AI-related stocks.

The weakness contributed to a broader Wall Street sell-off where the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 700 points, losing around 1.4%, while the S&P 500 dropped 1.9% and the Nasdaq Composite declined 2.5%. The relatively smaller losses in US stock futures suggested caution ahead of Nvidia's announcement as traders waited for financial results before making larger bets on technology stocks.

Beyond markets, economic uncertainty complicates the outlook: October retail sales and import price figures were scheduled to be released alongside Disney and Home Depot earnings, while the European Commission raised its 2026 euro area growth forecast to 1.4% from an earlier estimate of 1.1%, though it expects inflation to reach 3.2% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027 amid higher energy costs, shipping disruptions and pressure on refining and gas markets.
items.title: Nvidia's Q3 2026 Earnings Preview Amid Leadership Transition and Market Turbulence

items.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed a wave of recent technology disruptions to what he called ‘superintelligence’ — a term, per the reporting, given by President Donald Trump as a substitute for AI. The outages struck on Monday, November 16, when customers reported difficulty logging into major US banks including Wells Fargo, Chase, US Bank and Bank of America; that same day United Airlines suffered a broad system outage that briefly disrupted departing flights; and earlier in the week Microsoft 365 was rendered inaccessible. Appearing on Fox News, Mullin explained that modern systems face ‘a lot of technology thrown at us,’ noting that older backup systems are now overwhelmed by newer ones. He relayed an explanation from a tech expert — not Elon Musk — who suggested self-coding AI may have contributed to the breakdowns because legacy software is not built to keep pace with rapidly evolving, self-fixing programs; Mullin said this theory ‘kind of makes sense’ and described it as causing a ripple effect that overruns systems designed for slower operation. Defending the Trump administration’s handling of the failures, Mullin pledged federal resources to assist companies dealing with system breakdowns while asserting that national security remained intact and that responses would be swift.
items.title: DHS Secretary Blames 'Superintelligence' for Microsoft and US Banks Outage

items.summary: Hours after Chennai Super Kings (CSK) announced that MS Dhoni would serve as the team's mentor from IPL 2027, the former captain posted an emotional farewell video on Instagram. The nearly three-minute clip, set to the Bollywood song 'Main Har Ek Pal Ka Shayar Hoon' from the 1976 film Kabhi Kabhie and captioned 'Fans proved me wrong,' drew over 6.5 million likes within two hours of being shared. Dhoni's illustrious 19-year IPL career officially ended on Tuesday, marking a poignant conclusion to his tenure as CSK captain. His legacy with the franchise is substantial: he led CSK to five titles and two Champions League T20 trophies, remains the team's second-highest scorer with 5,314 runs, and holds the record for most appearances with 272. The video showcased a collection of pictures from his India playing days alongside teammates including Sachin Tendulkar, Yuvraj Singh, Virender Sehwag, Virat Kohli, Irfan Pathan, Anil Kumble, VVS Laxman, and RP Singh. Dhoni's captaincy was succeeded by Ruturaj Gaikwad in 2024, while team owner Rupa Gurunath revealed that he had hinted at his retirement months earlier during discussions on player retention ahead of the auction. His departure also recalls CSK's stint with Rising Pune Supergiant for a couple of seasons when they were banned from the IPL following the 2013 spot-fixing scandal, an episode that led to a life ban on then-CEO Gurunath Meiyappan.
items.title: MS Dhoni's IPL Retirement Video Breaks Internet; Records and Legacy Highlighted

items.summary:
India's digital payments industry is seeking help from Google to combat a growing form of Unified Payments Interface (UPI) fraud in which criminals exploit weaknesses at the Android operating-system level rather than simply deceiving users into sharing banking details. The National Payments Corporation of India, which operates UPI, has begun discussions with Google—according to a report by The Economic Times on 17 November—to strengthen security at that system level. This move follows concerns from payment companies that existing safeguards may be insufficient against fraudsters who gain access to a user's phone through malicious applications and system-level permissions.

Historically, most UPI fraud warnings have centered on familiar tactics such as sharing one-time passwords (OTPs), revealing UPI PINs, scanning fake QR codes, or approving payment requests from unknown senders. The emerging threat is different: criminals are finding ways to access phones and payment apps without users necessarily realizing what is happening. Some attackers use harmful applications—including those installed outside official app stores—to gain control over parts of a device by misusing Android permissions such as the 'display over other apps' feature, which lets an application appear on top of another in use. This can allow a malicious layer to capture information entered when someone opens a payment app and enters their UPI PIN.

The concern is that payment applications may not always be able to identify or block these attacks because the problem originates within the phone's operating system itself, creating risks that individual UPI apps cannot fully address. Payment companies have therefore pushed for stronger Android-level safeguards after raising concerns about fraud cases that could also expose them to financial liability. One suggestion from a payment industry official is to place stricter limits on applications installed through APK files from sources outside trusted app stores, with additional checks before such apps receive access to sensitive features like accessibility services, device administration and screen overlays.

Cybersecurity expert Narasimhan Elangovan of Ascentium India noted that improving Android security is only part of the solution; payment companies will also need to strengthen their own systems to identify suspicious activity and prevent unauthorised transactions. The discussions remain at an exploratory stage, with no confirmed public timeline for when any proposed changes would be introduced.

For users, the development underscores that UPI fraud extends beyond sharing an OTP or PIN—with application installation methods and granted permissions now affecting payment safety. Users are advised to avoid installing APK files shared through unknown links or messages and to exercise caution when granting apps permission to access other applications, control device functions, or view on-screen information. Separately, the Reserve Bank of India's fraud-awareness material warns about remote-access and screen-sharing applications that criminals can exploit to view or control devices and carry out unauthorised transactions.
items.title: NPCI turns to Google to address Android-level UPI fraud vulnerabilities as criminals exploit system permissions

items.summary: Nvidia announced on Tuesday that it has created a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance, following reports concerning former CEO Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of links to the illegal diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, alongside fellow board members Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. It is expected to meet at least once every quarter and work with independent third-party legal, national security and trade compliance experts to strengthen the company's existing oversight efforts while safeguarding national security without hindering technological innovation. Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones described the move as a positive step toward establishing a robust framework that uses available tools to protect national security while supporting continued innovation. The announcement comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's chip exports to China, where its advanced chips are in high demand for cloud computing and data centres powering the artificial intelligence industry but remain subject to US export restrictions. Reports questioning Huang's relationship with the businesswoman—who previously headed Singapore-based Megaspeed International—have raised concerns about potential national security risks and oversight of the company's chip exports. The move was welcomed by US President Donald Trump, who called it a good idea during a photo opportunity in Manila on Tuesday evening alongside leaders of Australia, India and Japan.
items.title: Nvidia Establishes National Security Oversight Committee Amid Chip Export Scrutiny

items.summary: Apple has introduced a new authentication method for the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone and most expensive phone ever made, which adds facial recognition unlocking via the front-facing camera based on simpler visual traits rather than the sophisticated 3D mapping used by conventional Face ID. This update addresses an early buyer complaint that the device's Touch ID fingerprint reader is not as smooth or fast as Face ID found on other iPhones. The feature was introduced in a beta version of Apple's iOS 27.3 operating system released Monday, taking an approach similar to the recently launched HomeView smart display. Because it is less secure than standard Face ID, users are cautioned that the convenience comes with trade-offs requiring mindfulness about security. Built-in safeguards require the phone to have been recently unlocked via Touch ID or a lock screen PIN for facial recognition to work, and Touch ID remains necessary for Apple Pay and other scenarios such as accessing passwords. The iPhone Duo was unveiled in September and represents the biggest single design change to the iPhone in nearly two decades of history. A separate beta update lets users automatically lock the phone when the inner screen closes instead of leaving the outer display active—helping avoid accidental taps and battery drain—but this option is disabled by default and requires opting in.
items.title: Apple Adds Face Unlock to iPhone Duo in iOS 27.3 Beta, Addressing Key Drawback

items.summary: Speaking at the 29th edition of the three-day Bengaluru Tech Summit, themed 'AI and Beyond,' Microsoft India and South Asia President Puneet Chandok argued that adopting artificial intelligence is only the easy part—delivering tangible impact on the ground remains the harder challenge. He urged businesses and leaders not to wait for AI to settle down before embracing it, drawing a parallel with ISRO's history: in 1981, the space agency hired a bullock cart for Rs 150 to transport equipment needed to test a satellite antenna because it lacked adequate transportation facilities. Chandok recalled that five hours later the problem was solved and decades later India reached the Moon—not via limousine or sophisticated vehicle, but in a humble bullock cart; had ISRO waited for perfect conditions, he noted, India would still be waiting today. Applying this lesson to AI, he said many leaders told him they wanted it to settle down first, but 'AI is not going to settle down,' and if the technology works for 1.5 billion people across India's 22 official languages, it will work for the world. Chandok highlighted Shiksha Copilot, a collaborative research project by Microsoft Research India and the Sikshana Foundation that helps teachers in Karnataka plan lessons in English and Kannada using context drawn from local children's lives; citing a study conducted last month among more than 1,000 teachers in Karnataka, he said the tool saved teachers two hours every week. He stressed that computing infrastructure alone would neither make India AI-ready nor unlock the technology's full potential—people matter most—and announced Microsoft is investing USD 20.5 billion and training 20 million Indians in AI by 2030. Framing AI as 'the new frontier,' Chandok likened it to a river that will not stop flowing, reminding listeners that Bengaluru has long been central to India's technology journey—turning to the city when software was needed and serving as mission control when India reached the Moon—and called on the city to ensure the world turns to Bengaluru once again.
items.title: Microsoft India Chief Urges Embracing AI Now Rather Than Waiting for It to Settle Down at Bengaluru Tech Summit

items.summary: At Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 on Tuesday, Infosys co-founder S Gopalakrishnan urged software engineers to focus on reviewing, debugging and certifying artificial intelligence (AI)-generated code as automation reshapes the technology industry. He noted that programming had become one of the first major activities affected by AI, warning that engineers would need stronger technical expertise to assess machine-generated software rather than rely entirely on automated coding tools. Gopalakrishnan cautioned that AI-produced code could contain errors, security vulnerabilities and unintended access points, so professionals must develop the ability to evaluate code before approving its implementation. He suggested employers might test graduates by presenting them with AI-written programmes and asking whether the software was suitable for deployment, reasoning that such assessments reveal understanding of programming principles and problem identification. Reviewing code, he stressed, demands deeper technical knowledge than simply generating it; engineers must learn to identify bugs, correct mistakes, integrate software with existing systems and certify its reliability. Drawing a comparison with doctoral education, Gopalakrishnan highlighted the importance of peer review and critical evaluation in this process. He also cautioned that major enterprises would not replace established technology systems with AI-generated software overnight, since organisations adopt changes gradually to ensure compatibility with legacy infrastructure while preparing documentation and training employees. Maintaining that AI would not eliminate demand for established IT services companies, Gopalakrishnan pointed out that businesses rely on outsourcing partners for specialised industry knowledge and experience gained across multiple clients. He cited Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro and Infosys as firms offering expertise spanning banking, healthcare, insurance and pharmaceuticals, arguing this broader exposure helps clients adopt practices internal technology teams may lack. Expecting consulting and outsourcing services to remain important for the foreseeable future, he also noted that AI could create opportunities for emerging companies to develop new technology products and services.
items.title: Infosys Co-Founder Urges Software Engineers To Master Code Review And Debugging Amid AI Automation

items.summary: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) responded to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, questioning the historic destruction of Halebidu and challenging him to identify those responsible for ransacking the Hoysala capital. In a retweet of Gandhi's post, BJP asked whether he knew why Dwarasamudra came to be known as Halebidu, meaning 'old capital,' and demanded that he name who had destroyed it. The party stated it could: Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur in 1311, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's army in 1326-27—and asked whether Gandhi could shame them. BJP also pointed to the damaged sculptures at the Hoysaleshwara Temple complex, noting that idols of gods still stand with broken faces and hands, asking who broke them before adding 'Satyam comes first in Satyam Shivam Sundaram.' This exchange followed Rahul's earlier post on X, in which he criticized BJP and RSS supporters amid controversy over his remarks about his parents' relationship. Gandhi said fear, anger and hatred had woven a web in the hearts of BJP and RSS supporters that stops them from experiencing and expressing love, adding that as a true Hindu it was his duty to free them from this web so they could experience 'the breathtaking beauty and joy of love and belonging,' ending with 'Satyam Shivam Sundaram.' The sculpture he referred to depicts Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati riding Nandi. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma also criticized Gandhi's post, saying no human being—including anyone from the Gandhi family—could be equated with God. Sarma argued that portraying mortals as Shiv and Parvati is not devotion but entitlement grown so arrogant it believes itself divine, stressing humility as the foundation of greatness. The political row came a day after Rahul's remarks about his parents, Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi, at the launch of his mother's memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love.
items.title: BJP counters Rahul Gandhi over Hoysaleshwara Temple post; Assam CM joins criticism amid controversy rooted in remarks on his parents' relationship

items.summary: Several Indian states have proposed reforms to the national medical entrance examination system, suggesting that students be allowed to attempt the NEET-UG exam more than once a year and that Class 12 board examination scores receive some weightage in admissions. These proposals were submitted to a high-powered task force led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, which is currently examining reforms to national-level examinations, according to news agency PTI citing sources. The panel was initially expected to submit its report by October 2026, but the government has granted it additional time as consultations with stakeholders remain underway. This reporting appears in a piece authored by Aastha Jha of The Times of India, who covers politics and business for the outlet.
items.title: States' Suggestions on NEET-UG Attempts and Class 12 Weightage to Nilekani Panel

items.summary: On the moving sandbars along the Teesta river in West Bengal, migrant farmers grow seasonal crops that are increasingly drawing elephants from adjacent forests. As these animals feed on the cultivated harvests, they bring people and wildlife into close contact. The river’s shifting course brings floods and erosion that continually reshape the sandbars, compelling farmers to relocate their fields and adjust to a changing landscape. Elephants track the seasonal crops seasonally and return repeatedly to the same areas to forage. In this arrangement, farmers lose crops, have their homes damaged by elephants, and endure sleepless nights guarding their fields. Despite years of coexisting with these animals, however, they receive no formal compensation for crop losses.
items.title: Migrants and elephants contend over shifting sandbars of Teesta in West Bengal
